outcome: Artin's primitive root conjecture remains open and unproven unconditionally for any single value of a; since 26 January 2024 there have been three genuine advances that move the surrounding landscape without settling the stated existence question: (1) Klurman-Shparlinski-Teräväinen (Dec 2024) proved the predicted asymptotic density holds unconditionally for almost all a in a growing range, improving Stephens (1969); (2) Goldmakher-Martin-Peringuey (Feb 2025) proposed refined conjectures capturing finer distributional properties, proved under GRH plus unconditional weaker versions; (3) Murty-Naik (Aug 2026) gave a conditional proof of the full conjecture assuming a new 'non-abelian large sieve inequality' they themselves cannot yet prove, plus partial unconditional progress toward that inequality. None of these is a resolution or even a settled case (no single a is unconditionally known to be a primitive root for infinitely many primes); all are best classified as progress on the surrounding theory.
summary: The stated bullet is Artin's conjecture on primitive roots (posed 1927): for integer a, not a perfect square and not −1, are there infinitely many primes p with a as a primitive root mod p? This is still open in full generality and, as the current Wikipedia article states, 'there is no single value of a for which Artin's conjecture is proved' unconditionally (Heath-Brown 1986 only shows at least one of {2,3,5} works, a disjunctive result, itself pre-dating the window). Three pieces of work since the 26 Jan 2024 cutoff bear on the surrounding theory. (1) Klurman, Shparlinski and Teräväinen, 'On Artin's conjecture on average and short character sums' (arXiv:2412.13355, submitted 17 Dec 2024, published in Bull. LMS), prove unconditionally that the Artin asymptotic holds for almost all a up to exp((log log x)^2) — an average-case, not a general or per-a, result; it does not settle the existence question for any specific a, so per §3.1 an 'almost all' statement about an infinitude/existence question does not change the stated bullet, though it is a genuine improvement to the surrounding average-case theory and so counts as progress. (2) Goldmakher, Martin and Peringuey, 'Refinements of Artin's primitive root conjecture' (arXiv:2502.19601, Feb 2025), propose finer conjectures on the distribution of ord_p(a) that specialize to Artin's conjecture, proving them under GRH and proving unconditional weaker versions; this refines rather than resolves the conjecture. (3) Murty and Naik, 'A non-abelian large sieve and Artin's primitive root conjecture' (arXiv:2608.21573, submitted 21 Aug 2026), claim a proof of the full conjecture conditional on a new 'non-abelian large sieve inequality' that is itself an open conjecture, plus some unconditional partial progress toward that inequality via duality techniques. This is a conditional proof analogous in spirit to Hooley's 1967 GRH-conditional proof — a genuine new conditional pathway, but not an unconditional resolution, and (being one month old at the time of this research) has not yet been digested by experts or seen any recorded reaction. None of the three papers mentions any AI or machine-learning system in their methods or acknowledgements — all are traditional human-authored analytic number theory. Separately, Artin's conjecture appears as 'Sample Problem 1' (Tier 3, authored by Olli Järviniemi) in the FrontierMath AI benchmark (Glazer et al. 2024, arXiv:2411.04872), but that benchmark problem asks for a specific computable density constant (⌊10^6 d_∞⌋ for primes where ord(2)>ord(3)) built using Artin-conjecture-style machinery, not the open existence conjecture itself — it is a related/variant well-posed numeric question, not a case of the stated bullet, and no source found indicates any AI model has actually solved it (aggregate FrontierMath scores are reported per-tier, not per-problem, and public commentary — e.g. Terence Tao's remark that Tier 3 problems would 'resist AIs for several years' — treats it as unsolved). No genuine case or resolution of the conjecture has any AI involvement; the only AI connection found is benchmarking, not mathematical progress on the stated problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the Klurman-Shparlinski-Teräväinen 'almost all a' result deserves `partial` rather than `progress`, on the reading that it settles the conjecture for a genuine (density-1-in-a-growing-range) subset of a-values. I did not adopt this because the underlying claim for each such a is still an infinitude-of-primes statement whose truth for that specific a is not established with certainty (it is a statement about the counting function's asymptotic matching the conjectured constant for almost all a, which is compatible with but does not by itself prove Artin's conjecture holds for those a — the density result is itself already conjectured as a corollary if Artin's conjecture were true, and proving it unconditionally for almost all a is more precisely a conditional-removal/quantitative average result than a case-by-case existence resolution). Given the ambiguity, a reader could reasonably classify this as `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` instead.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the Klurman-Shparlinski-Teräväinen paper's precise theorem statement to determine whether 'the asymptotic holds for almost all a' logically implies 'a is a primitive root for infinitely many p' for each such a (versus only implying the counting function's growth rate matches, which is a slightly weaker statement), and any expert digestion or citation record of the Murty-Naik paper once it has had time to be reviewed.
